title: How to Hire a Freelance Ruby on Rails Developer
description: A practical guide to hiring a freelance Rails developer: what to write in a job post, what to ask in interviews, red flags to watch for, and how contracts should work.
keywords: hire freelance ruby on rails developer, hire rails developer, find rails contractor, hiring freelance developer, rails developer hourly rate
body:
Most bad freelance experiences are decided before any code is written. They happen because the client and the developer both had a different picture of the project in their heads, neither of them wrote it down, and they discovered the gap six weeks in.

This guide is written for the client side. I have been on the other end of these conversations, and the pattern is consistent enough to be predictable.

Before you write a job post

The most useful thing you can do happens before you contact anyone: write the project down.

Not a feature list. A description of what the software does, in sentences.

“Customers search for available rooms for two dates, we hold the room for ten minutes while they pay, we take a card payment, and they get an email confirmation. Staff see the same bookings in an admin area and can cancel them.”

That paragraph is worth more than fifty bullet points, because it exposes the real complexity. It hints at availability logic, a timeout, payment integration, transactional email and an authorisation model — all things a fifty-item feature list would have hidden under vague words like “calendar” and “payments”.

Then do the highest-leverage exercise available: decide what is not in version one. Every feature you defer is money and weeks saved. Most projects succeed because of what they left out, not because of how well they were built.

What a good job post contains

  • What the product does and who uses it
  • The existing stack, if there is one
  • The engagement model: fixed scope, hourly, or ongoing
  • The timeline you have in mind, and whether it is fixed or flexible
  • The time zone overlap you can genuinely work with
  • How you want to communicate: calls, async written updates, or both
  • What “done” looks like

Notice what is not on the list: your budget, unless you have a real range and are comfortable stating it. Filtering candidates on budget before knowing the scope is how good developers get screened out of projects they would have done well.

What to ask in the first conversation

Most hiring mistakes are made in a thirty-minute call. These are the questions that surface the important information.

“Walk me through something you built that is similar.” Listen for specifics, not adjectives. “I built a booking system” tells you nothing. “We had a double-booking problem under load, so I moved availability checks into a transaction with a row lock” tells you they have dealt with a real system.

“How do you decide what is in scope?” A good answer involves asking you questions and pushing back on parts of the request. A bad answer is “whatever you want.” If they never push back, they will not push back on a deadline either.

“What does your testing look like?” Any credible answer includes automated tests. “I test manually” is a complete answer and it should end the conversation for anything that will be maintained.

“Who owns the code and the accounts?” Everything — the repository, the hosting, the domain, the database, the third-party accounts. Under your organisation, from the first commit. If a developer wants to keep access to your infrastructure after the project ends, that is a serious red flag.

“What happens if the project needs to change halfway through?” You want to hear about a change-order process, not “we would just handle it.” Scope changes are normal. Undocumented scope changes are how projects go badly.

“Can you give me a reference or show me the live product?” Every serious freelancer can. If they cannot, ask why.

Red flags

Guaranteed timelines with undefined scope. Anyone who can promise a date before understanding the project is guessing.

No questions about your requirements. A developer who does not ask what the users actually do has not thought about the product.

Hourly with no estimate. Hourly billing with no scope and no estimate has no ceiling. If they will not give you a range, they have not thought about the work.

Pressure to start immediately. “I have capacity this week, can we sign today” is a sales tactic. Good developers are busy and will not be destabilised by you not deciding today.

Everything is a full-time commitment. Be suspicious of anyone who cannot describe what else they are working on. A freelancer with no other clients is either between projects or telling you something untrue.

Refusing to break the work into milestones. All-at-once payment for a multi-month project puts all the risk on you and removes any leverage to finish. Milestones are not distrust; they are the standard.

Rates

For a competent freelance Ruby on Rails developer in 2026, expect roughly:

  • $60–$100/hour for a strong generalist
  • $100–$150/hour for someone with specific Hotwire Native, Rails performance or security expertise
  • $30–$60/hour for developers earlier in their careers or in lower-cost markets

Two warnings.

First, a rate that is dramatically below the market is not a bargain. It usually means less experience, or a plan to raise the price mid-project once you are dependent.

Second, the cheapest quote is rarely the cheapest project. I have watched clients pay $25/hour, then spend forty hours on a codebase nobody else wanted to maintain. The hourly saving evaporated and the schedule slipped anyway.

For fixed-scope work, judge on the total price and the quality of the scope, not the implied rate.

Contracts: what should be in them

You do not need a lawyer for a $20,000 project. You do need a written document covering:

  • Scope — what is being built, specifically enough that both of you would recognise it
  • Deliverables — what you receive and when
  • Milestones and payment — amounts and dates, with a schedule
  • Revision policy — how many rounds of changes per milestone, and how additional work is priced
  • Change process — how scope changes are agreed and billed
  • Code ownership — you own everything, from the first commit
  • Confidentiality — mutual, and it should survive the end of the project
  • Termination — how either side exits, and what happens to work in progress

A shared document with a scope, a price and a date is dramatically better than no document. Legal review is worth it for contracts above roughly $50,000 or where you are dealing with something unusual.

The engagement models

Fixed scope, fixed price. The best default once the requirements are clear. Aligns incentives and gives you a predictable number. Requires both sides to have genuinely agreed the scope first.

Hourly. Right for audits, maintenance, exploratory work, and anything where you do not yet know what the answer is. Wrong for building something whose scope you have not thought through.

Ongoing retainer. A block of hours each month. Good for teams shipping continuously who want steady capacity without a hiring cycle. Make sure the terms let you stop.

Consultation first. A short, fixed-fee engagement that produces a written assessment before any implementation. It costs you a few thousand dollars, and it is the cheapest risk reduction available. You keep the document whether or not you continue.

How to run the work once you have hired someone

Use a repository with proper history from day one. Commits, branches, pull requests. If the code is in a zip file, that is already a bad sign.

Get written weekly updates. Short, factual, what shipped, what is blocked, what is next. This catches a drifting schedule in week two rather than week eight.

Make decisions quickly. The most common cause of delay is client-side indecision, not technical difficulty. If you can decide in a day what would take a week to deliberate, say so and hold yourself to it.

Test at the end of each milestone, not at the end of the project. Discovering a misunderstanding in week two costs a conversation. Discovering it in week ten costs a rewrite.

Review the code. You are paying for a codebase someone else will maintain. If you have a technical stakeholder, they should read some of it. If nobody on your side can read it, that is worth knowing early.

What a good freelance relationship looks like

The best engagements I have had share a few things: the scope was written down, the client decided quickly, we talked weekly, and nobody was surprised. Problems surfaced early and were treated as information rather than as blame.

If that is what you are looking for, tell me about your project. I will give you a straight answer about whether I am the right fit, and a real number rather than a discovery-call fee that goes nowhere.

title: Hotwire Native vs React Native
description: Hotwire Native lets you ship iOS and Android apps from one Rails codebase. Here is how it compares to React Native on speed, native feel, cost and long-term maintenance.
keywords: hotwire native vs react native, hotwire native, rails mobile app development, hybrid mobile app framework, rails ios and android app
body:
If your web application is already in Rails and you need it on iOS and Android, you have three realistic options: build two native apps, build one React Native app, or use Hotwire Native. The third is newer and far less discussed than the other two, so this post is mostly about how it actually performs in production rather than what the launch posts claimed.

What Hotwire Native actually is

Hotwire Native is an open-source framework from the 37signals team behind Rails and Basecamp. It is a native iOS and Android shell that renders your existing Rails views.

There is no JavaScript bundle, no component tree and no second codebase. Your Rails routes map to native screens, your ERB templates render as screens, and Turbo Frames handle navigation. The shell handles the native chrome: navigation bars, tab bars, modals, the app icon, push notifications, app store distribution.

You write Rails. You ship an app.

How it compares on the things that matter

Time to first release

This is where Hotwire Native wins decisively, and it is not a small margin.

A React Native app needs: a React codebase, a Node toolchain, native build configuration for both platforms, a bridge to your Rails API, a design system implemented in React Native components, and someone who can debug a JavaScript error through a native stack trace.

Hotwire Native needs: a native shell (included), your existing Rails app, and a navigation mapping file. The work is in the Rails app you already have.

For MisrPrime I shipped an e-commerce platform where the same Rails controllers and views back both the responsive website and the iOS and Android apps. The mobile-specific work was a navigation config and a handful of view variants — not a second application.

How it feels to use

This is the fair criticism, so let me be precise.

A Hotwire Native screen is a web view. It is fast — you are loading small partials over a local bridge, not full pages — but it is not a native view hierarchy. If you compare a Hotwire Native screen against a pure SwiftUI screen with identical layout, you can see the difference. In practice, for a booking flow, a catalogue, an account area or an admin tool, users do not notice.

What you give up is the ability to use platform-specific widgets that have no web equivalent. A live-activity lock screen widget, a native share sheet with a custom preview, a drag-to-rearrange table with system animations. These are possible via native bridges, but you are back to writing native code, at which point you should ask whether you want two apps.

Push notifications and offline

Push notifications work well — you register for them, get a device token, and hand it to your existing Rails backend. This is a genuine advantage over a lot of hybrid setups, because the notification logic stays in the same codebase as the rest of your application logic.

Offline is the weak point, and I will not pretend otherwise. Hotwire Native does not give you a full offline-first data layer. There is workarounds, and there is a good deal of research still happening in this area. If your product must function fully with no connectivity — a field-service app, an inspection tool, a logistics driver app — plan for that explicitly rather than discovering it late.

The JavaScript question

Hotwire Native uses Hotwire’s JavaScript (Turbo and Stimulus), not React. You get some JavaScript, but it is dramatically less than a React Native app, and none of it is bundled by a Node toolchain.

For a team that is strong in Rails and weak in JavaScript, this is the difference between a project they can ship and a project they cannot.

Long-term maintenance

The maintenance argument favours Hotwire Native strongly, and this is the part most comparisons skip.

With React Native, every dependency you add is a native dependency. A library that has not been updated for two years may not build against the current Xcode or Android Gradle Plugin. You are exposed to the churn of the entire native ecosystem.

With Hotwire Native, the native shell is thin and stable. Most of your application is Rails code, maintained on the Rails release cycle. You are exposed to far less.

That does not mean it is free. You will still deal with App Store review, Xcode version bumps and Android API level changes. But the surface area is much smaller.

When to choose Hotwire Native

Choose it when:

  • Your web app is already in Rails and is good
  • The mobile app is a companion to that web app, not a standalone product
  • You have a small team and need to ship
  • Your team is stronger in Rails than in JavaScript
  • You are extending an existing product rather than starting from scratch

When not to choose it

Choose something else when:

  • You are starting from zero and the app is the product, not a companion
  • You need genuinely native interaction patterns — games, AR, complex gestures, offline-first field work
  • You have an existing React or React Native team and codebase
  • You need deep native integrations (background location, complex Bluetooth, advanced camera work)
  • You need to be in app stores with a fully native-feeling UI benchmarked against the platform’s own apps

The honest summary

Hotwire Native is the right answer more often than its search volume suggests, and the wrong answer less often than its enthusiasts claim. It is a genuinely good fit for “we already have a great Rails app and want it on phones,” which describes a large share of the projects I am asked to build.

It is not a universal replacement for React Native, and any comparison that claims otherwise has not shipped one.

If you have a Rails application and are weighing up mobile, tell me about it — I will give you a straight answer about whether Hotwire Native fits or whether you would be better off elsewhere.

title: How to Speed Up a Ruby on Rails App
description: A practical guide to Rails performance: finding N+1 queries, fixing them, using the query cache, adding indexes, and the caching layers worth the complexity.
keywords: speed up rails app, rails n+1 query, rails performance optimization, rails caching, slow rails application
body:
A Rails application that is slow at scale is almost never slow because of Ruby. It is slow because of the database.

Ruby executes in the region of a few million simple operations per second. Your application’s response time is spent waiting for PostgreSQL, and the number of round-trips you make dominates everything else you could optimise. Fix the queries and the page gets fast. Micro-optimise the Ruby and nothing visible happens.

This is the order I work in, and it is the order I would recommend.

Step 1: measure before you change anything

Do not guess. Two tools will tell you almost everything you need.

Bullet, by Magician. It wraps N+1 detection, unused eager loading, missing eager loading, and duplicate queries, then prints a visual waterfall when it finds them:

# Gemfile, group :development
gem "bullet"
# config/environments/development.rb
Bullet.enable = true
Bullet.raise = true # fails the request so you cannot ship the N+1

Set Bullet.raise = true in development. It converts a silent N+1 into a failed request, which means it gets fixed rather than forgotten.

Scout or AppSignal, for production. Bullet does not run in production. A slow query that only appears under real data volume needs a real APM to find.

Step 2: the N+1 query

This is the single most common performance defect in Rails, and it is trivially fixable once you recognise it.

You have a list of posts, each belonging to a user:

@posts = Post.all

In your view:

<% @posts.each do |post| %>
  <p><%= post.user.name %></p>
<% end %>

That looks like one query. It is not. Rails runs one query to fetch the posts, then one more for each post’s user. Ten posts means eleven queries. A thousand posts means one thousand and one — and it gets worse with every user you add.

Fix it by telling Active Record what you need:

@posts = Post.includes(:user)

Now it is two queries, always, regardless of list size.

You can also let Bullet find them for you, or look for the tell-tale sign in logs: a query with WHERE "users"."id" = $1 repeated dozens of times.

The subtler version happens through a method call rather than a view. If post.user is called inside a before_action, scope, presenter or serializer, the fix looks the same but the location is harder to find. includes still works.

Step 3: indexes

An unindexed foreign key is a table scan. On a table with 100,000 rows, that is the difference between 2ms and 400ms.

Foreign keys are indexed by default in Rails through references. If you used belongs_to correctly, your foreign keys are already indexed. The ones that are usually missing:

# The slow version: filtered on status, ordered by created_at
Post.where(status: "published").order(created_at: :desc)

# Add a composite index in the right order — equality columns first
add_index :posts, [:status, :created_at]

Column order in a composite index matters enormously. Postgres can use an index for equality conditions on a prefix of the columns, then filter the rest. So [:status, :created_at] serves both “all published posts” and “published posts newest first”. [:created_at, :status] only serves the second.

Check what is actually happening:

EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM posts WHERE status = 'published' ORDER BY created_at DESC;

If you see Seq Scan on a large table, that is your missing index.

Step 4: the query cache

Rails ships a query cache that de-duplicates identical read queries within a single request. It is on by default.

It does not survive across requests, because your data changes between them. For anything read-heavy, cache deliberately.

Rails.cache.fetch("featured_posts", expires_in: 10.minutes) do
  Post.published.includes(:user).limit(10)
end

For read-mostly reference data that changes daily, cache it much longer:

# config/initializers/cache_store.rb — for apps on one server
Rails.cache.configure do |config|
  config.default_cache = :memory_store  # NOT for multi-server: each server gets its own copy
end

If you run more than one application server, use a shared store. Redis or Memcached. An in-memory store on a two-server deployment gives you two different caches, which is a class of bug that only appears in production.

Step 5: stop loading columns you do not use

A model with 80 columns, of which the page needs 6, is transferring 74 columns you are throwing away.

# Only select what the view uses
Post.select(:id, :title, :published_at).includes(:user)

For large text columns this matters a great deal. For most tables, honestly, it does not. Measure before you complicate your code.

Step 6: count efficiently

Model.count on a large table is a full scan unless Postgres can satisfy it from statistics.

# Slow on huge tables
Post.count

# Fast — uses a maintained statistics table
Post.approximate_count(column: :id)

# Or keep an exact cached counter
Post.count_cached

approximate_count uses reltuples and can be slightly stale. For a “1,234 posts” label on a page, that is entirely fine.

Step 7: paginate properly

Model.all with 10,000 rows loads 10,000 rows to render 20.

Post.includes(:user).page(params[:page]).per(25)

The trap is eager loading across a large association. If you eager load posts and their users, then paginate, Postgres still has to join the whole set before limiting. For large datasets, paginate the ids first, then eager load the page:

ids = Post.published.order(created_at: :desc).limit(25).offset(params[:offset]).pluck(:id)
@posts = Post.includes(:user).where(id: ids)

Step 8: fragment and HTTP caching

For markup that is identical for every user, cache the rendered fragment:

<% cache ["sidebar", Sidebar::VERSION] do %>
  <%= render "shared/sidebar" %>
<% end %>

Sidebar::VERSION is a constant you bump when the partial changes. This is the part people get wrong — cached fragments with no version key serve stale content until someone notices and nobody can explain why.

And set real HTTP caching headers. A static asset or a page that is the same for everyone should have a max-age in the tens of minutes or hours, not zero.

What is usually not worth optimising

  • Ruby-level micro-optimisation. Rewriting a loop in a more “efficient” style on a page that spends 400ms waiting on the database changes nothing.
  • Memoising instance variables in views. Saves microseconds, adds coupling, and the readability cost is real.
  • Switching frameworks. If the answer is “it is slow in Rails”, the answer is almost never “it would be faster elsewhere”. It would be equally slow there.

A realistic order of operations

If you inherit a slow Rails application, this is what I do:

  1. Turn on Bullet in development, fix every N+1 it finds
  2. Check EXPLAIN on the five slowest queries from your APM
  3. Add the missing composite indexes
  4. Add caching to the three slowest pages
  5. Check for SELECT * on wide tables
  6. Only then look at anything else

In my experience the first two steps fix 80% of the problem. A Rails application with disciplined queries and correct indexes is fast enough for the overwhelming majority of products.

If your application is slow and you want someone to look at it properly, get in touch. I offer a fixed-fee Rails performance audit where you get a written list of what is slow, what it will take to fix, and what it will cost — whether or not you hire me to do the work.

title: Ruby on Rails vs Django: Which to Choose?
description: Ruby on Rails and Django both ship the same architectural ideas. Here is where they genuinely differ — syntax, ORM, async, admin interfaces, and which to pick.
keywords: rails vs django, ruby vs python web framework, rails or django, django vs rails performance, python vs ruby backend
body:
Rails and Django are the two frameworks you will hear compared most often after Laravel, and for good reason: both were built around the idea that a web framework should make decisions for you rather than asking you to assemble one. Django came first, and Rails is partly a response to it — which is why the resemblance is so strong.

They agree on nearly everything architectural. The differences are real but narrower than the framework tribalism suggests.

Where they are genuinely the same

Both are full-stack MVC frameworks. Both use convention over configuration. Both ship an ORM, a migration system, a templating layer, a routing layer, a test layer, an admin interface, and a security model that is safe by default. Both are designed for a relational database with a domain of meaningful complexity.

If you have built in one, the conceptual transfer to the other is close to free. The directory structure, the request lifecycle, the “where do I put this” question — the answers map onto each other almost one to one.

This is a mature comparison. There is no architectural gotcha waiting to surprise you in either direction.

Syntax and language

Rails is Ruby, and the framework leans on Ruby’s expressiveness. Implicit objects, blocks, metaprogramming, and a metaprogramming-friendly API:

class Booking < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :customer
  scope :upcoming, -> { where(check_in: Date.today..) }
end

Django is Python, and it favours explicitness and type hints:

class Booking(models.Model):
    customer = models.ForeignKey(Customer, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    check_in = models.DateField()

    class Meta:
        ordering = ["check_in"]

Python’s type hints are the significant difference here. With mypy or pyright, a large Django codebase can be type-checked end to end, and IDE support is excellent. Ruby’s ecosystem has RBS and Sorbet, but neither is close to as widely adopted. If your organisation mandates static typing, that is a genuine practical advantage for Django.

The other side: Ruby’s scope and its block-based query composition are more compact than anything idiomatic in the Django ORM. You can write a query builder that reads cleanly in Rails in a way that takes more ceremony in Django.

The ORM

Rails’ Active Record is the active record pattern: one class per table, instances map to rows, and the model carries both data and behaviour.

Django’s ORM is an identity map: model classes are definitions, and instances are in-memory objects mapped to rows via an explicit manager layer. The distinction matters more than it sounds — it means Django models do not hold unsaved state, and the save/refresh boundary is explicit rather than implicit.

RailsDjango
Query syntaxPost.where(published: true).includes(:user)Post.objects.filter(published=True).select_related("user")
Single objectPost.find(1)Post.objects.get(pk=1)
CreatePost.create!(title: "x")Post.objects.create(title="x")
N+1 preventionincludes / preloadselect_related / prefetch_related

select_related is a SQL JOIN for belongs-to and has-one; preload_related is a separate query for many-to-many and reverse relations. That maps closely onto includes, which does both, and Rails also has the more explicit preload and eager_load if you want to be precise.

Both are mature and neither is a performance trap if you use them. Both suffer identically if you do not.

Async support

This is the sharpest current difference.

Django has native async views, async ORM methods, and good ASGI support. For a genuinely I/O-bound workload — many concurrent external API calls, streaming, high fan-out to third-party services — Django’s story is now straightforward.

Rails has worked on this for years. Async and Enumerator::Lazy exist, and a Rails application can serve requests concurrently on modern servers with threaded or fiber-based handling. But async Rails is still not as ergonomic or as well-trodden as Django’s. If your architecture is “make 200 concurrent HTTP calls and stream the results back,” Django is the smoother choice today.

For a conventional database-backed application, this changes nothing. Neither framework’s advantage here affects your users.

The admin interface

Django wins this decisively, and it is Django’s strongest argument. django.contrib.admin gives you a full CRUD interface over your models — searchable, permissioned, filterable — in about five lines:

admin.site.register(Booking)

It ships in the framework, it is genuinely good, and it is why a large number of Django projects exist primarily to power an internal tool.

Rails’ ActiveAdmin is the closest equivalent, and it is excellent — but it is a gem you add rather than a component you inherit, and you write some configuration to get a good result. Rails also has better options for customer-facing admin areas, where you want a designed interface rather than a utilitarian one.

If your product is an internal tool with a small external surface, Django’s admin is a meaningful head start.

Templating and front-end

Both ship a template language that is deliberately not a full frontend framework. Both have a first-party answer for interactivity that is increasingly the default.

Rails has Hotwire — Turbo for page navigation and Turbo Frames for partial updates, plus Stimulus for the small amount of custom JavaScript. This is now the default way Rails applications are built, and it is genuinely good. A Rails application can be fully interactive with no build step and no single-page app.

Django has HTMX integration through third-party packages, and the broader Django ecosystem leans on HTMX plus Alpine.js. Django also has the option of pairing with a separate React or Vue frontend via a REST API, which is what a lot of Django projects do.

The practical difference: Hotwire is first-party and versioned with Rails. HTMX for Django is a community integration, well maintained, but not the same guarantee.

Performance

Effectively identical for the workloads these frameworks target. Both are dynamically typed, both are dominated by database time, and both are fast when the queries are disciplined and slow when they are not.

If you want the argument, the Rails performance guide applies almost line for line to Django — the N+1 problem, indexes, the query cache, and the same conclusion that the database is what matters.

The ecosystem and jobs market

Python is much larger, and it is the strongest argument for Django. Python is a general-purpose language with a huge footprint in data science, ML, automation and backend. If your team already writes Python, Django is a natural fit, and the pool of people you can hire from is far wider.

Rails engineers are more specialised. Ruby is a web language in practice, and almost all Ruby developers are Rails developers. This cuts both ways: the pool is smaller, but the median Rails developer has chosen to be in web development rather than drifted there from data science.

The practical difference shows up in agency work. If you need a developer for six months on a Rails application, staffing is slower and more expensive. If you need one for six months on a Django application with a data component, staffing is much easier.

Which should you choose

Rails, when: you want the most integrated full-stack experience with the least assembly; you are building a product with a rich domain and Hotwire’s default approach fits it; you have a Ruby team; or you want Rails’ opinionated consistency to scale across a growing codebase.

Django, when: you already have a Python team; you need a genuinely excellent admin interface out of the box; you have ML, data or scientific Python components that need to share code with the web layer; or you need native async for a specific I/O-bound workload.

Either, when: you are building a conventional web application and have no other constraints. The choice will not determine whether you succeed, and switching later is expensive but rarely necessary.

My honest take

If nobody tells me anything about your project and asks me to pick, I would pick Rails for a new product and Django for an internal tool with a Python data pipeline attached.

That is not because Django is worse. It is because Rails is a more complete answer to “build me a web application,” and a Django project ends up assembling its front-end story from parts while a Rails project gets one that works.

If you are weighing this up for something specific and want the reasoning applied to your situation, get in touch.

title: Ruby on Rails vs Laravel: Which Should You Pick?
description: A developer-to-developer comparison of Rails and Laravel covering syntax, performance, jobs market, ecosystem and the types of project each handles best.
keywords: rails vs laravel, ruby on rails vs php laravel, laravel vs rails comparison, rails or laravel, php vs ruby framework
body:
Rails and Laravel are the two frameworks I get asked to compare most often, usually by someone who knows one of them and is mildly suspicious of the other. This post is written for that person.

They are genuinely close in architectural philosophy — both are opinionated, convention-heavy, full-stack frameworks that assume an MVC structure and give you sensible defaults for nearly everything. The resemblance is not a coincidence; Rails influenced Laravel significantly.

Syntax and ergonomics

Rails favours implicit objects and metaprogramming:

class Booking < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :customer
  has_many :guests, dependent: :destroy

  validates :check_in, presence: true
  scope :upcoming, -> { where(check_in: Date.today..) }
end

Laravel favours explicit facades and constructor injection:

class Booking extends Model
{
    protected $fillable = ['customer_id', 'check_in'];

    public function customer(): BelongsTo
    {
        return $this->belongsTo(Customer::class);
    }
}

Both are readable. The difference is philosophy: Ruby hides more behind convention, PHP spells more out explicitly. Teams that like explicitness tend to be happier in Laravel. Teams that like terseness tend to be happier in Rails. Neither is more correct.

One genuine difference: Ruby’s blocks and Rails’ scope make query composition feel natural in a way that is harder to replicate in PHP without leaning on the query builder heavily. If you write a lot of complex scopes, you will notice.

Performance

Both are dynamically typed and both are roughly the same speed for database-backed work. As with Rails versus Node.js, the runtime language is not what determines your response time — the number of queries and whether they are indexed is.

Where they differ slightly:

  • Rails has the better story on connection handling and connection pooling with modern adapters, and CRuby’s threading improvements since 3.0 have closed most of the historical gap.
  • Laravel has the advantage of OPcache, which is available on essentially every shared host and cheap VPS. Rails needs a decent application server, and a cheap host may be a poor fit. If you are deploying to a $5/month shared host, PHP is meaningfully easier.

Deployment and hosting

This is where the difference is most concrete and least discussed.

PHP deploys by copying files. There is no build step to speak of, no bundler, no compiled assets beyond what your build tool produces. Any host that runs Apache or nginx and PHP runs your Laravel app. This is why Laravel has far broader hosting availability.

Rails needs Ruby installed, a version manager, Bundler, a precompiled asset pipeline, and a real application server — Puma or Passenger behind nginx. This is a few hours of setup, not a weekend, but it is real infrastructure.

Modern Rails deployment is genuinely pleasant — Kamal for a single server, or a managed platform. But “runs anywhere PHP runs” is still a substantial advantage for Laravel, particularly for small teams without a DevOps person.

MySQL vs PostgreSQL is a related point. Laravel’s historical home is MySQL, and a lot of Laravel tutorials and packages assume it. Rails defaults to PostgreSQL and the ecosystem reflects that. If your team already knows MySQL deeply, that matters more than framework syntax.

The jobs market

This is the most consequential difference and the one clients care about most.

PHP is far larger. If you are staffing a team of twenty, the PHP developer pool is much bigger. This is not close in most markets.

But the PHP market is bifurcated. There is a large volume of WordPress and legacy PHP work, and a smaller pool of people who write modern Laravel well. The median PHP developer and the median Laravel developer are different people.

Ruby is much smaller and considerably more concentrated. Ruby developers are more likely to be professional engineers working on well-maintained codebases. The pool is small enough that hiring takes longer and salaries are higher.

My observation across client projects: PHP teams are easier to staff and hit a capability ceiling sooner. Ruby and Rails teams are harder to staff and hit that ceiling later.

If you are a solo developer or a team of two or three, the jobs market is irrelevant — you are not hiring. Weight this section at zero.

Ecosystem

Both have first-party answers to the common problems: mail, background jobs, file storage, WebSockets, admin interfaces, authentication, encryption, asset pipelines.

Rails’ answer is generally more integrated and more opinionated. Rails 8 goes further with Solid Queue, Solid Cache, Solid Cable and Solid Mail — the first-party versions of infrastructure that used to require a separate Redis and a separate service. This is a meaningful reduction in moving parts.

Laravel’s ecosystem is bigger and more varied, with strong first-party options (Queued jobs, Horizon for Redis queues, Livewire for reactive interfaces, Filament for admin panels). Laravel arguably has the better admin panel tooling available in any language, with Filament being a serious piece of work.

One Laravel-specific strength: Livewire gives you reactive interfaces with no JavaScript, in a way that is more approachable than Hotwire for teams coming from a PHP background. If your team finds Stimulus and Turbo mental effort, that is a real consideration.

Project fit

Choose Rails when: you have a relational domain with real complexity, you value a strong default stack with few decisions, you are building something long-lived that another team will maintain, and you can afford a slightly narrower hiring pool.

Choose Laravel when: you are deploying to shared hosting or a constrained environment, you are staffing a large PHP team, you want the best available admin panel tooling, or your team’s existing expertise is PHP.

Choose neither when: your problem is genuinely simple. Both frameworks have more in them than you need, and a well-structured application built on a smaller framework — or even server-rendered templates — will serve you better than an underused Rails or Laravel app.

The honest summary

These are close enough that “Rails is better” or “Laravel is better” is not a defensible claim. Rails has better-integrated infrastructure and a more opinionated, consistency-producing philosophy. Laravel has broader hosting, a larger hiring pool, and excellent admin tooling.

If your team already knows one, stay on it. The framework is rarely the constraint — and switching is one of the most expensive forms of technical debt to take on voluntarily.

If you are weighing a specific project and want a view from someone who builds in both, get in touch.

title: Ruby on Rails vs Node.js: How to Choose in 2026
description: A practical comparison of Ruby on Rails and Node.js covering development speed, runtime performance, hiring, and the types of product each one suits best.
keywords: ruby on rails vs nodejs, rails vs node, should I use rails or nodejs, ruby vs javascript performance, rails vs express comparison
body:
Choosing between Ruby on Rails and Node.js is one of the decisions that quietly determines how fast your team ships for the next three years. Both are excellent. They are good at different things, and the popular arguments about which is “faster” mostly miss the point.

This is the comparison I wish I had when I started picking frameworks for client projects, written from the perspective of someone who ships production applications in both.

The short answer

If you are building a typical web application — database, user accounts, payments, an admin panel, a public marketing site — choose Rails. You will have a working, correct version in less time, and you will spend that saved time on the parts of your product that actually differentiate it.

Choose Node.js when you have a specific reason to: a team that already knows it deeply, a heavily real-time or streaming workload, or a dependency graph that is Node-first.

Everything below is the reasoning behind that.

Development speed is where Rails wins, and it is not close

Rails was designed around the idea that convention beats configuration. A new developer can open a Rails codebase and predict where things are, because the framework makes strong decisions for you.

A basic CRUD resource — model, controller, routes, migrations, validations, and a working index page — is one scaffold command away:

rails generate scaffold Booking customer:references room:references check_in:date check_out:date total:decimal

You get migrations, a model with validations, a controller with the standard seven actions, views, and routes. In Express you write all of it.

This compounds. Consider a feature like “a user can book a room, we check availability, charge a card, and email a confirmation.” In Rails you are assembling existing, well-understood pieces: ActiveRecord associations, a transaction around the availability check, Stripe’s Ruby gem, and a mailer. Each piece is boring and predictable. The feature takes an afternoon.

The same feature in Node means choosing an ORM (or writing queries), picking a validation library, wiring a job queue for the email, and being more deliberate about transaction boundaries. It is all doable. It just costs more decisions, and decisions are what slow teams down.

Runtime performance is closer than the internet suggests

The “Node is faster because it’s V8 and Ruby is slow” argument comes from a benchmark that measured empty-loop throughput. It is not relevant to your application.

What matters is response time, and response time in a database-backed web application is dominated by:

  1. The number of queries you make
  2. Whether those queries have indexes
  3. Network round-trips to your database
  4. Time spent serialising and rendering

All four are framework-independent. A Rails app with three indexed queries will beat a Node app with thirty unindexed ones, every time. Conversely, if both teams write disciplined data access, the gap narrows to single-digit percentages that no user will ever notice.

Ruby did have a genuine concurrency weakness historically, but MRI gained real parallel threading in Ruby 3.x, and CRuby 3.4 improved it further. If concurrency at extreme scale is your primary concern, that is a legitimate reason to look at Node — but it is a much narrower reason than “it’s faster.”

What Rails genuinely does better

Batteries included, and maintained. Active Record gives you migrations, associations, validations, callbacks and connection management. Action Mailer, Active Job, Action Cable and Active Storage are all first-party. You are not assembling a framework out of forty packages.

Convention that scales. A six-person team all writing in Rails style produces code that looks like it was written by one person, because the framework led them there. This is the single biggest maintainability advantage of Rails, and it is invisible until you inherit a codebase written without it.

Security defaults. Strong parameters, CSRF protection, escaped output by default, and a well-maintained security team. You can still write an insecure Rails app. It is harder to do accidentally than in most stacks.

Background jobs. ActiveJob with Sidekiq, Solid Queue or Delayed Job gives you a clean abstraction over your queue. In Node you are choosing between BullMQ, Bee-Queue, Agenda and pg-boss, each with different semantics.

What Node genuinely does better

Real-time and streaming. WebSocket-heavy applications, collaborative editors, media processing pipelines and anything where you’re shuttling events rather than rendering documents. Node’s event loop model is a natural fit and Rails needs more deliberate architecture here.

The JavaScript talent pool. If you are hiring a team of ten engineers tomorrow, there are far more JavaScript developers available than Ruby developers. In a specific, well-paid market like London or San Francisco, that difference shrinks considerably — but in a remote-first search it is real.

Sharing code with the frontend. If your frontend is already React and you want to share types and validation logic, TypeScript lets you do that in one codebase. Rails gives you this via a separate TypeScript package and Hotwire if you want it, but it is not seamless.

Ecosystem reach at the edges. If a core dependency of your product is a JavaScript library, you can use it directly rather than finding a Ruby port or a WASM wrapper.

A decision framework

Ask these four questions in order:

Does your team already know one of them deeply? This outweighs everything else on this page. A senior Rails developer will out-produce a mediocre Node developer indefinitely, and vice versa. Institutional knowledge beats framework preference every time.

Is your workload request/response or event/stream? Request/response with a relational database — the majority of software — favours Rails. Event/stream favours Node.

Are you optimising for speed to first release? Rails. The gap is weeks, not days.

Is hiring your binding constraint? If you need to staff a large team quickly and have no existing expertise, Node is the safer bet.

A note on the hybrid approach

The most common pattern I see in successful products is not “pick one” — it is a Rails application that talks to a separate Node service for one specific realtime or media-processing responsibility. Rails owns the domain, the database and the user-facing application. Node owns the thing Node is genuinely better at.

This is a good architecture when you have a real reason for it. It is a bad architecture when it is just framework envy, because you now run two deployment pipelines, two dependency trees and two on-call rotations.

What I would choose today

For a new product with a database and a team of any size up to about fifteen engineers: Rails.

For a product whose core value is real-time collaboration, live media, or high-volume event processing: Node, and probably not Rails at all.

For a codebase that already exists in either stack: stay in it. The switching cost is almost never worth the theoretical gains, and the framework is rarely what was actually holding you back.

If you are still deciding and want a second opinion on your specific situation, get in touch — I would rather spend thirty minutes on a call than quote you a project that is the wrong shape.

title: How Much Does a Web Application Cost in 2026?
description: Real cost ranges for web and mobile applications in 2026, broken down by project type, team composition and hourly rates. Includes the costs people forget to budget for.
keywords: how much does a website cost, web application development cost, how much to build an app, freelance developer rates, custom software cost
body:
“How much will my app cost?” is the question I am asked most, and the honest answer is more useful than the one clients usually want to hear: it depends almost entirely on scope, and the range for any given project is wide.

What I can do is give you real numbers from real projects, explain what drives them, and flag the costs people forget to budget for. Those forgotten costs are frequently larger than the development itself.

Realistic ranges by project type

These are 2026 figures for a competent team, based on what I charge and what I see in the market.

Project typeTypical costTimeline
Marketing site, 5–8 pages, CMS$3,000 – $12,0002–4 weeks
Small business web application$12,000 – $30,0006–10 weeks
SaaS MVP with billing and accounts$30,000 – $80,0003–5 months
Booking or marketplace platform$40,000 – $120,0004–8 months
Native iOS and Android app$25,000 – $100,000+3–6 months
Existing codebase audit and fixes$2,000 – $8,0001–3 weeks

The number that surprises most people is the first one. A good marketing site is not a $40,000 project, and if you are being quoted that, ask what is included.

What actually drives the cost

Number of distinct screens

Not pages — screens. A booking platform with a search page has six to ten distinct states: loading, no results, partial results, availability conflict, price breakdown, payment, confirmation, error. Each one is design, build, test and edge-case work.

This is why “it’s just a booking form” is never just a booking form.

Integrations

Every third-party service is a project in miniature. Payments, email, SMS, maps, calendar sync, invoicing, accounting, a shipping API, an identity provider. Budget two to five days per straightforward integration, and considerably more for anything with an awkward API or a webhooks-that-fire-at-3am problem.

Integrations are also where scope quietly grows. One integration often reveals three requirements you did not know about.

Authentication and roles

“Users can log in” becomes “users log in, reset passwords, verify email, have roles, get invited by an admin, see different navigation per role, and lose access when suspended” before the first sprint ends. Budget for it up front.

Content and how it is managed

Who updates the text? If it is your developer, you have saved money. If it is a marketing manager on day one, you have bought a CMS, which is a real project of its own.

Quality expectations

This is the one clients rarely think about. There is a large gap between software that works in a demo and software that handles real users: error states, validation, rate limiting, backups, monitoring, email deliverability, accessibility, and the hundred small decisions that only matter once traffic arrives.

You are paying for this whether you budget for it or not. The only question is whether you pay for it deliberately or pay for it twice.

The costs people forget

This is the part that turns a $30,000 project into a $60,000 one. In rough order of how often they surprise people:

Hosting and infrastructure. $20 to $500 per month for a small application, more as traffic grows. Managed Postgres, object storage, a background job worker, error tracking, uptime monitoring. Not large, but it is never zero and it never stops.

Domain, email and transactional email. $15–$200 per year. Transactional email is the one that gets missed — you need a provider, and you need to authenticate your sending domain or your password reset emails will be marked as spam.

Payment processing. Stripe and similar charge roughly 2.9% plus $0.30 per transaction. Your margin needs to absorb this.

App store fees. 15–30% of in-app revenue, depending on platform and program. Apple and Google take a larger cut than web payments, and this materially changes your unit economics.

Maintenance. 15–25% of development cost per year after launch. This is not optional. Rails and its dependencies need security updates, the Ruby version needs moving, the database needs upgrading, and something will break at 2am.

Content. Copywriting, photography, product photography, video. Frequently 10–20% of the total project cost, and almost never in the original budget.

Legal and compliance. Terms of service, privacy policy, and — if you take payments or handle personal data across jurisdictions — real legal advice. A privacy policy generator is not legal advice.

Your own time. The most consistently underestimated cost. You will be required for decisions, content, testing and feedback. Founders regularly budget zero for this and then the project stalls for three weeks while they are busy with their actual job.

How to get an accurate quote

You cannot get an accurate quote from a description. You can get an estimate, and then narrow it. Here is the process that works:

Write down what the software does, in sentences, not features. “A user can search for available rooms between two dates, hold a room for ten minutes while they pay, and receive a confirmation by email.” That sentence is worth more than a fifty-item feature list, because it exposes the real complexity.

Decide what is not in version one. This is the highest-leverage thing you can do before contacting anyone. Every feature you defer is directly money and time saved. Most projects succeed because of what they left out.

Get a written scope, not a verbal estimate. Any competent developer will produce a document listing deliverables, a fixed price and a delivery date. If you cannot get that, they are guessing, and so are you.

Ask what they are assuming. A quote that does not state its assumptions is not a quote. “This assumes existing accounts system, no payment processing, content supplied by you” tells you far more than the number.

Reserve 20%. Not padding — the reality that the first version of anything surfaces requirements nobody anticipated. A project that delivers exactly the agreed scope with zero contingency is a project that hit a problem and someone absorbed it.

On hourly versus fixed price

Hourly makes sense for undefined work: an audit, ongoing maintenance, an emergency, exploratory work where you genuinely do not know what the answer is yet.

Fixed price makes sense once the scope is agreed. It aligns incentives — the developer is motivated to build it efficiently, and you have a predictable number.

The failure mode is fixed price on undefined work. The developer is now carrying the risk of scope you have not thought of, and the predictable outcome is either a change-order conversation or an under-built product.

What I would tell a friend

If you have $20,000 and a business idea, spend it on the smallest thing that tests whether anyone wants it. Not a beautiful version of your full vision — the crudest possible version that solves the one problem that matters.

Most projects fail because nobody wanted what was built, not because the code was not good enough. Finding that out for $8,000 is much better than finding it out for $80,000.

If you have a defined scope and want a real number rather than a range, send me the details. I will tell you what I think it costs, and if you are not the right fit for me I will say so and point you somewhere better.
